content: The trials included in this review were conducted across various countries, including three in Australia, four in Brazil, one in the Caribbean Islands, one in Denmark and Sweden, three in France, eight in India, four in Israel, four in Italy, two in South Africa, two in Sweden, twelve in the United Kingdom, five in the United States, and one in Venezuela. Five trials recruited women admitted to hospitals, while another five included both inpatients and outpatients. Eighteen studies recruited women from hospital outpatient clinics, one from urban antenatal clinics, and three from antenatal clinics with unclear hospital affiliations. Seven studies recruited women in hospitals but did not specify the setting, while 16 likely recruited in hospital settings, and three had unclear recruitment settings. The trials were published between 1968 and 2017, with most having small sample sizes (43 out of 58 trials included fewer than 130 women). The largest study involved 314 participants. Four studies included three treatment arms, while the rest had two arms. Only six studies had treatment arms with more than 100 women. The gestational age at trial entry varied: 21 trials included only women in their third trimester, 20 included women in their second and third trimesters, eight included women in their first and second trimesters, and nine did not report gestational age at entry. Among trials comparing antihypertensive drugs to placebo or no treatment, 11 recruited women before 32 weeks of gestation, two recruited women at 32 weeks or later, and 16 did not specify gestational age or disaggregate data by gestation. The severity of hypertension at trial entry varied due to differing inclusion criteria. Five trials did not define thresholds for mild to moderate hypertension. Women with severe hypertension (systolic ≥170 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg) were excluded. Eight trials included only women with proteinuria, 19 excluded women with proteinuria, 14 included women regardless of proteinuria status, and 17 did not report proteinuria at trial entry. Ten trials included only women with chronic hypertension, 22 excluded such women, 10 included women regardless of chronic hypertension status, and 16 did not mention chronic hypertension at trial entry. A variety of antihypertensive drugs and doses were used, all administered orally except for glyceryl trinitrate, which was given transdermally. Beta-blockers included acebutolol (400–1200 mg/day), atenolol (50–100 mg/day), labetalol (200–2500 mg/day in divided doses), mepindolol (5–10 mg/day), metoprolol (50–400 mg/day in one or two doses), oxprenolol (80–640 mg/day in one or two doses), pindolol (5–30 mg/day), and propranolol (30–160 mg/day). Alpha-agonists included methyldopa (250–8000 mg/day in one to four doses). Calcium channel blockers included amlodipine (5 mg/day), isradipine (10 mg/day in two doses), nicardipine (60 mg/day in three doses), nifedipine (20–160 mg/day), nimodipine (120 mg/day in six-hourly doses), and verapamil (720 mg/day in three doses). Alpha-blockers included prazosin (3–15 mg/day in three doses). Nitric oxide donors included glyceryl trinitrate (10 mg/day). Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors included sildenafil (60–150 mg/day in three doses). Direct vasodilators included hydralazine (50–100 mg/day). Some trials combined hydralazine with beta-blockers in the intervention group. The outcomes of pre-eclampsia and severe pre-eclampsia were defined differently across trials. Proteinuria/pre-eclampsia was generally defined as new proteinuria (≥1+ or ≥300 mg/24 hours), but some studies used higher thresholds (≥2+ or ≥5 g/24 hours). Other trials did not define pre-eclampsia criteria. Since the 2011 WHO recommendations on pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, this review has been updated twice (2014 and 2018), adding data from 12 trials (1627 women) and four antihypertensive drugs (oxprenolol, amlodipine, furosemide, and sildenafil). The 2011 recommendations included comparisons of any antihypertensive drug versus placebo/no drug, any drug versus methyldopa, and any drug versus calcium channel blockers. The 2018 update added a comparison of other antihypertensive drugs versus beta-blockers (19 trials). Maternal outcomes such as death, eclampsia, and severe pre-eclampsia were unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Severe maternal morbidity outcomes like HELLP syndrome and pulmonary edema were also unclear. Neonatal outcomes, including perinatal death and neonatal bradycardia, were similarly uncertain. Side effects and adverse events were inconsistently reported, with very low-certainty evidence for most outcomes. The British National Formulary (BNF) lists methyldopa and glyceryl trinitrate as safe in pregnancy. However, beta-blockers may pose risks of intrauterine growth restriction, neonatal hypoglycemia, and bradycardia. Nicardipine and verapamil may inhibit labor and cause maternal hypotension or fetal hypoxia. Furosemide is not recommended for gestational hypertension due to maternal hypovolemia. Drugs like nifedipine, amlodipine, nimodipine, prazosin, sildenafil, and hydralazine require careful consideration of risks and benefits. Women generally value a positive pregnancy experience, including effective clinical care, timely information, and emotional support. However, in low-resource settings, indirect costs and reliance on traditional practices may limit access to care. The intervention's acceptability may be influenced by awareness of hypertension risks and the need for daily medication adherence.
